title: Most Nearby Exoplanets May Harbour Life, but Mostly Microbial
site_name: BGNES: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
excerpt: The search for extraterrestrial life in the universe is unlikely to end anytime soon. Researchers at Northern Arizona University in the United States have developed complex planetary models suggest
content:
The potential life forms described in the study resemble the world of the Dune novels more than the aliens depicted in the Avatar films.

The search for extraterrestrial life in the universe is unlikely to end anytime soon. Researchers at Northern Arizona University in the United States have developed complex planetary models suggesting that 26 of 29 rocky exoplanets near Earth could support some form of life. Such life would likely be less advanced in evolutionary terms than life on Earth, although it may have emerged earlier. The differences are linked to the amount of energy supplied by vegetation.

The scientists found evidence suggesting that life on three of the exoplanets studied may have progressed beyond the simplest microbial stage. The study was published in September in the International Journal of Astrobiology and reported by The Debrief. According to the researchers, life on one of the planets may even have surpassed life on Earth in certain respects.

The potential life forms described in the study resemble the world of the Dune novels more than the aliens depicted in the Avatar films.

“If life on these exoplanets evolved in the same way as it did on Earth, most of them would probably be inhabited only by microbes rather than alien creatures,” said lead author Chris Doughty.

The university team believes a shortage of energy derived from plants could explain why complex life has not developed on these planets. On Earth, warmer and wetter conditions favour abundant vegetation, which provides a major food source for many animals.

A Shortage of Photosynthesis

Most rocky exoplanets discovered by astronomers orbit red dwarfs, which are relatively small and cool stars. Planets in the habitable zones of such stars are generally tidally locked, meaning the same hemisphere constantly faces the star. As a result, only half of their surfaces receive direct starlight.

“The total amount of photosynthesis over a year is probably lower because the light is weaker and only half of the planet's surface is available for photosynthesis,” explained Michael Gowanlock, a computer science lecturer and co-author of the study.

The researchers modelled 29 potentially habitable exoplanets, including TRAPPIST-1e, located about 40 light-years from Earth. They compared the amount of carbon absorbed by vegetation on these worlds with the levels accumulated on Earth before and after the emergence of vascular plants. Their aim was to determine which planets receive enough energy from plant life to support animal life.

The results indicate that TRAPPIST-1e has accumulated only 21% of the amount of carbon absorbed on Earth, “even though it is several billion years older than our planet”, the researchers noted.

The team identified only two exoplanets, GJ 1061c and K2-3d, where life could potentially have reached a more advanced stage earlier than it did on Earth. Both are larger, warmer and brighter than most Earth-like planets in our cosmic neighbourhood.

The models suggest that on three other planets, life may have reached a stage comparable to that on Earth during the age of the dinosaurs. However, these worlds are likely to have drier conditions.

Nevertheless, the researchers believe that if life exists on most of the planets studied, it is probably limited to microbes. Observations by the James Webb Space Telescope may allow their conclusions to be tested more precisely.

For now, the findings provide no grounds for believing that complex extraterrestrial life exists in our immediate cosmic neighbourhood. | BGNES
